source.title: Can Mamba Learn How to Learn? A Comparative Study on In-Context Learning Tasks
source.authors: Jongho Park; Jaeseung Park; Zheyang Xiong; Nayoung Lee; Jaewoong Cho; Samet Oymak; Kangwook Lee; Dimitris Papailiopoulos

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares width/depth configurations at fixed parameter groups and measures ICL regression loss, a different setting and measure from language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: Only V4 is tested: Appendix C varies depth and width at fixed parameter groups for linear-regression ICL. The FLOPs plots measure task-specific ICL loss, not held-out language-model pretraining loss or a fitted power law. Scaling-law statements and results cited from other work are not this study's results; synthetic-language perplexity comparisons do not test scaling laws.
record.test_reason: The study compares Transformer, Mamba and hybrids on synthetic ICL tasks trained from scratch. It borrows Kaplan et al.'s FLOPs-counting convention but never measures held-out language-model pretraining loss or fits a power law. The Appendix C width/depth ablation measures linear-regression ICL squared loss, not LM pretraining loss. So it does not test V4, which concerns language-model pretraining loss, or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase covers only the appendix ablation. The authors' main conclusions are that Mamba can perform ICL comparably to Transformers on standard regression tasks and outperforms them on sparse parity, but struggles on vector MQAR retrieval and decision trees. The hybrid MambaFormer matches or beats both across their ICL suite. Appendix C adds that very shallow and very deep-narrow models struggle, and that AdamW with a scheduler helps (more for Mamba/MambaFormer) without changing these conclusions.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models from scratch on synthetic ICL tasks and compares task loss across architecture configurations; it does not reproduce language-model pretraining scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Width and depth affect linear-regression ICL performance; optimizer and schedule also affect performance, with larger benefits for Mamba and MambaFormer than Transformer.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed non-embedding parameter count, 2-layer Transformers fail to learn linear-regression ICL. 128-layer narrow models of all three architectures also struggle. Mamba shows a weaker shallow penalty, and MambaFormer learns with 2 layers. Results are figure-only (Figure 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth/width shape at fixed parameter count materially affects loss on synthetic in-context regression tasks trained from scratch, with architecture-dependent thresholds.

record.problems: For the tested shape comparison, the text provides qualitative descriptions rather than numerical values or uncertainty estimates for the Figure 10 configurations. Results concern synthetic ICL regression, not held-out language-model pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results meeting the claim-version criteria were left out. Other ICL-task plots and synthetic-language perplexity tables do not test scaling-law behavior or the width/depth loss claim as defined here.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining-loss power law in N, D or C is measured or fitted.
All: no extrapolation of fitted laws.
All: shape is varied only for synthetic linear-regression ICL loss, not LM pretraining loss.
All: no power-law fits in any regime.
All: no relation of downstream performance to scale or pretraining loss is fitted.
All: no exponents or fitting choices examined.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T2' with V4 'challenges' overreaches. The ablation was done to choose model configurations for ICL comparisons, on synthetic regression loss, not LM pretraining loss. The FLOPs x-axis plots show the best model per FLOPs per architecture, with no power-law fit. Kaplan et al. is cited for the FLOPs-counting convention and for the claim that ICL improves as training loss falls.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation as compute changes.
Held-out language-model pretraining loss; generality beyond the tested ICL linear-regression configurations.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predicting downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, and bending from a power law.
